title: VegVault Database Structure
text:
Currently, VegVault 2.0.0 consists of 34 interconnected tables with 123 fields (variables), and 1 view (a stored query that combines tables), which are described in detail below. However, the internal database structure may not be directly relevant to most users, as the {vaultkeepr} R package processes all data to output only the most relevant information in a “ready-to-analyze” format.

[!NOTE]
For Most Users: If you’re primarily interested in using VegVault for research, you may want to start with our Usage Examples rather than diving into the technical database structure.

This section provides comprehensive documentation of all tables and their relationships for users who need detailed technical information about the database architecture.



The diagram shows every table with its columns and the links between tables; it is drawn from the schema with R/Website/render_schema_diagrams.R, as are the diagrams of the single tables below. The colour of a table’s header marks its section: brown for datasets, samples and taxa, teal for traits, olive for abiotic data and the links to gridpoints, light brown for the references, and black for the authors and the record of each build.








Several tables contain metadata and administrative information that are not directly linked to the scientific data:

Authors: Information about VegVault authors and maintainers, including contact details
version_control: Database version information with descriptions of changes over time and, from v2.0.0, how each version was built
BuildProducers: the input files of each build, one row per data file type, with the tag of the data release it was read from
sqlite_stat1 & sqlite_stat4: SQLite system tables containing database index statistics for query optimization

The Datasets table represents the main organizational structure in VegVault, serving as the keystone for managing and organizing all data. Each Dataset contains one row with a unique Dataset ID (dataset_id), Dataset name (dataset_name), geographic location (coord_lat, coord_long), Dataset Type (dataset_type_id), Dataset Source (data_source_id), Dataset Source Type (data_source_type_id), and Sampling Method (sampling_method_id).

The Dataset Type defines the most basic classification of each Dataset, ensuring that the vast amount of data is categorized systematically. Currently, VegVault contains the following types of Datasets:

vegetation_plot: This type includes contemporary vegetation plot data, capturing contemporary vegetation characteristics and distributions.
fossil_pollen_archive: This type encompasses past vegetation plot data derived from fossil pollen records, providing insights into past vegetation and climate dynamics.
traits: This type contains functional trait data, detailing specific characteristics of plant species that influence their ecological roles.
gridpoints: This type holds artificially created Datasets to manage abiotic data, here climate and soil information (a Dataset Type created to hold abiotic data, see details in the Database Assemly).

VegVault maintains detailed information about the primary data source, thereby enhancing the findability and referencing of primary data sources. Each Dataset is derived from a specific Source-Type that provides detailed information on the source used to retrieve the original data. The current Source-Types in VegVault include:

BIEN - Botanical Information and Ecology Network
sPlotOpen - The open-access version of sPlot
TRY - TRY Plant Trait Database
Neotoma-FOSSILPOL (source type FOSSILPOL in the database) - The workflow that aims to process and standardise global palaeoecological pollen data. Note that we specifically state Neotoma-FOSSILPOL and not just Neotoma, as FOSSILPOL not only provides the data acquisition but also alters it (e.g., creating new age-depth models). It also addresses major challenges in paleoecological data integration, such as age uncertainty, by incorporating probabilistic age-depth models and their associated uncertainty matrices. This enables the propagation of temporal uncertainty in subsequent analyses, a critical advancement for robust macroecological studies, previously flagged as a major issue with paleo-data.
gridpoints - artificially created Datasets to hold abiotic data. See Database Assembly for more details.

Sampling methods vary significantly across the different types of Datasets integrated into VegVault, reflecting the diverse nature of the data collected. Such information is crucial for understanding the context and limitations of each Dataset Type. For contemporary vegetation plots, sampling involves standardised plot inventories and surveys that capture detailed vegetation characteristics across various regions. Fossil pollen data are collected from sediment records from numerous different depositional environments representing past vegetation. Therefore, information on sampling methods is only available for both vegetation_plot and fossil_pollen_archive Datasets, providing metadata that ensures accurate and contextually relevant analyses.

To support robust and transparent scientific research, each Dataset in VegVault can have multiple references at different levels. The Dataset Source-Type, Dataset Source, and Sampling Method can all have their own references, providing detailed provenance and citation information. This multi-level referencing system enhances the traceability and validation of the data. Each Dataset can also have one or more direct references to specific data, further ensuring that users can accurately cite and verify the sources of their data.

This means that one dataset can have one/several references from each of those parts. Let’s take a look at an example of what that could mean in practice.
We have selected the dataset fossilpol_1001 (dataset ID 91184 in this version), Hail Lake in Yukon, which is a fossil pollen archive. Therefore, it has the reference of the Dataset Source-Type:

Flantua, S. G. A., Mottl, O., Felde, V. A., Bhatta, K. P., Birks, H. H., Grytnes, J.-A., Seddon, A. W. R., & Birks, H. J. B. (2023). A guide to the processing and standardization of global palaeoecological data for large-scale syntheses using fossil pollen. Global Ecology and Biogeography, 32, 1377–1394. https://doi.org/10.1111/geb.13693

and reference for the individual dataset:

Grimm, E.C., 2008. Neotoma: an ecosystem database for the Pliocene, Pleistocene, and Holocene. Illinois State Museum Scientific Papers E Series, 1.







Samples represent the main unit of data in VegVault, serving as the fundamental building blocks for all analyses. There are currently 12,459,714 Samples in VegVault 2.0.0 (of which 1,569,221 are gridpoints of abiotic data, see Database Assembly).
VegVault encompasses both contemporary and paleo data, necessitating accurate age information for each Sample. Contemporary Samples are assigned an age of 0, while Samples from fossil pollen records are in calibrated years before the present (cal yr BP). The present is here specified as 1950 AD.


The table contains one Sample per row, with each Sample containing: a unique Sample ID (sample_id), Sample name (sample_name), temporal information about Sample (age), sample site (size of the plot if available; sample_size_id), and additional information about sample (sample_details; this is currently not being used). As VegVault encompasses both contemporary and paleo-data, accurate age information is required for each Sample.

Each taxonomic name undergoes an automated classification (see Database Assembly) and results are stored in the TaxonClassification table. To classify the diverse taxa present in the VegVault database, the {taxospace} R package was used. This tool automatically aligns taxa names with the Taxonomy Backbone from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, providing a standardized classification framework. Specifically, we try to find the best match of the raw names of taxa using the Global Names Verifier. Two kinds of names are corrected by hand after the automatic classification: fossil pollen types that combine two or more taxa, and the pollen type “Pinus Picea” (see Database Assembly).

Taxonomic classification for some Taxa might be only available down to the genus or family level, while most of the data is classified to species level. Classification information, detailed up to the family level, is stored for each taxon, ensuring consistency and facilitating comparative analyses across different datasets. Currently, the VegVault database holds 109,220 taxonomic names, of which we were unable to classify only 900 (0.8%).

The table contains one Trait per row, with each Trait containing: a unique Trait ID (trait_id), original Trait name from primary source (trait_name), and Trait Domain (trait_domain_id). Traits are grouped into Trait Domains to allow for easier aggregation of Traits across data sources. As there are differences in trait names across sources of data and individual Datasets, the VegVault database contains Trait Domain information to group traits together. In total, 6 Trait Domains are present: Diaspore mass, Leaf Area, Leaf mass per area, Leaf nitrogen content per unit mass, Plant heigh, and Stem specific density, following Diaz et al. (2016). The names are stored as in VegVault 1.0.0, including the spelling Plant heigh for plant height. Yet, it is up to the user to decide how to further aggregate trait values if multiple trait Samples of one Trait Domain are available for the same environmental or taxonomic entity.

In general, data of functional traits of vegetation taxa follow the same structure of the Dataset and Samples obtained directly from the Dataset Source-Types. Therefore, TraitsValue table contains not only the actual measured value of Trait observation but also information about linking information across Datasets, Samples, and Taxa. This comprehensive linkage ensures that each Trait value is accurately associated with its relevant ecological, environmental and taxonomic context.
Since VegVault 2.0.0, every trait value is stored in the unit of its Trait Domain (trait_unit of TraitsDomain), shown in the table below. Each value references exactly one versioned conversion rule of TraitUnitConversion and, when it is derived from another trait, one derivation rule of TraitDerivation, such as the reciprocal that turns specific leaf area (SLA) into leaf mass per area (LMA). The values and units as the data providers reported them are not stored in the database; they are part of the trait data release (VegVault-Trait_data), together with the audit tables of the conversion.

The abiotic data in the VegVault database provide essential information on environmental factors affecting vegetation distribution and traits. Currently, VegVault includes abiotic data from CHELSA, CHELSA-TRACE21, and the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD) v2.2. CHELSA and CHELSA-TRACE21 provide high-resolution climate data, while HWSD offers detailed soil information. VegVault 1.0.0 named the soil source WoSIS; it was HWSD v2.0 or v2.01 (the exact version was not recorded).


As VegVault contains abiotic variables from several primary sources, the AbioticVariable table contains descriptions of abiotic variables (abiotic_variable_name), their units (abiotic_variable_unit), and measurement details (measure_details). These data include variables such as climate and soil conditions, which are crucial for understanding the ecological contexts of vegetation dynamics.

Some properties of the values need attention:

bio4 (temperature seasonality) is in hundredths of a degree Celsius, as its unit says; in VegVault 1.0.0, the present-day bio4 was 0 south of about 65.7° N because of a truncated download.
A present-day bio12 (annual precipitation) of 6553.5 kg m-2 is the storage limit of CHELSA V2.1, so it is a lower bound.
CHELSA-TRACE21 stores precipitation in whole kg m-2, so a dry quarter with less than 0.5 kg m-2 is 0 in the past (bio18, bio19), while the present-day values come in steps of 0.1.
In the Sahel and the Sudanian belt, the coldest quarter of bio19 can be the dry winter in one product and the rainy season in the other, so bio19 can change between 0 and several hundred kg m-2 between the present day and the past.

Gridpoints are stored in artificially created Datasets and Samples, with one Dataset holding more Samples only if they differ in age. We store the link between gridpoint and non-gridpoint Samples as well as the spatial and temporal distance. A link is kept when the two are at most 50 km and at most 5,000 years apart, and any gridpoint Sample without a link is discarded as not relevant for the vegetation dynamics.
Since VegVault 2.0.0, the links are stored once per position, a distinct combination of longitude, latitude and age, because many Samples share a position. The References table is a central component that serves all sections of the VegVault database. This table contains all References, independent of the source of the reference and the type of data. Each row contains a single Reference, which is then linked to the type of data which is being referenced. The Dataset Type defines the most basic classification of each Dataset, ensuring that the vast amount of data is categorized systematically. Currently, VegVault contains the following types of Datasets:

vegetation_plot: This type includes contemporary vegetation plot data, capturing contemporary vegetation characteristics and distributions.
fossil_pollen_archive: This type encompasses past vegetation plot data derived from fossil pollen records, providing insights into past vegetation and climate dynamics.
traits: This type contains functional trait data, detailing specific characteristics of plant species that influence their ecological roles.
gridpoints: This type holds artificially created Datasets to manage abiotic data, here climate and soil information (a Dataset Type created to hold abiotic data, see details in the Database Assemly).

VegVault maintains detailed information about the primary data source, thereby enhancing the findability and referencing of primary data sources. Each Dataset is derived from a specific Source-Type that provides detailed information on the source used to retrieve the original data. The current Source-Types in VegVault include:

BIEN - Botanical Information and Ecology Network
sPlotOpen - The open-access version of sPlot
TRY - TRY Plant Trait Database
Neotoma-FOSSILPOL (source type FOSSILPOL in the database) - The workflow that aims to process and standardise global palaeoecological pollen data. Note that we specifically state Neotoma-FOSSILPOL and not just Neotoma, as FOSSILPOL not only provides the data acquisition but also alters it (e.g., creating new age-depth models). It also addresses major challenges in paleoecological data integration, such as age uncertainty, by incorporating probabilistic age-depth models and their associated uncertainty matrices. This enables the propagation of temporal uncertainty in subsequent analyses, a critical advancement for robust macroecological studies, previously flagged as a major issue with paleo-data.

Samples represent the main unit of data in VegVault, serving as the fundamental building blocks for all analyses. There are currently 12,459,714 Samples in VegVault 2.0.0 (of which 1,569,221 are gridpoints of abiotic data, see Database Assembly).
VegVault encompasses both contemporary and paleo data, necessitating accurate age information for each Sample. Contemporary Samples are assigned an age of 0, while Samples from fossil pollen records are in calibrated years before the present (cal yr BP). The present is here specified as 1950 AD.

Currently, VegVault includes abiotic data from CHELSA, CHELSA-TRACE21, and the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD) v2.2. CHELSA and CHELSA-TRACE21 provide high-resolution climate data, while HWSD offers detailed soil information. VegVault 1.0.0 named the soil source WoSIS; it was HWSD v2.0 or v2.01 (the exact version was not recorded).


As VegVault contains abiotic variables from several primary sources, the AbioticVariable table contains descriptions of abiotic variables (abiotic_variable_name), their units (abiotic_variable_unit), and measurement details (measure_details). title: VegVault Database Structure
text:
The References table is a central component that serves all sections of the VegVault database. This table contains all References, independent of the source of the reference and the type of data. Each row contains a single Reference, which is then linked to the type of data which is being referenced. This allows a single Reference to be used across data types, but also one data point having many different references.
Moreover, most primary sources of the data have a license, which requires correct attribution. Therefore, each Reference has information if such a Reference needs to be cited while using the specific data.

title: Data Assembly Process of VegVault 2.0.0
text:
VegVault v2.0.0 has been assembled through systematic integration of multiple publicly available databases, each contributing specialized data types to create a comprehensive vegetation database spanning both temporal and ecological dimensions. Each data source is processed in its own repository and released with a tag, and the database is built from these tagged files only.
The assembly workflow visualization:











Primary data sources:

Neotoma Paleoecology Database - Fossil pollen data (0-20,000 years BP)
sPlotOpen - Contemporary vegetation plots
BIEN - Contemporary vegetation and functional traits
TRY Plant Trait Database - Comprehensive plant functional traits
CHELSA - High-resolution climate data (contemporary and paleoclimate)
Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD) v2.2 - Global soil data (VegVault 1.0.0 named this source WoSIS)

Data Processing: Individual processing pipelines for each data type using specialized GitHub repositories

VegVault-FOSSILPOL v2.0.0 - Fossil pollen data processing
VegVault-Vegetation_data v2.0.0 - Contemporary vegetation processing
VegVault-Trait_data v2.0.0 - Functional trait data processing
VegVault-abiotic_data v2.0.0 - Environmental data processing
VegVault v2.0.0 - Consolidation into unified SQLite database structure with key steps:

Taxonomic Harmonization: Using the {taxospace} R package to align taxa with GBIF backbone
Trait Categorization: Grouping traits into functional domains following Díaz et al. (2016)
Spatial-Temporal Linking: Creating gridpoints for abiotic data and linking to vegetation samples

VegVault database - The released SQLite database (see Database Access)




All VegVault processing repositories use GitHub Tags to ensure complete reproducibility. For v2.0.0, every input file of the build is pinned by repository, tag, file name and SHA-256 checksum in Data/Producers/producer_manifest.yml, checked against its data specification before the build, and listed with its tag in the table BuildProducers of the database. The table version_control of the database records the build profile, the git commit of the code and the checksum of the pin manifest, enabling exact replication of the database assembly process.





Fossil pollen records have been downloaded from the Neotoma Paleoecology Database using their API on 19th November 2026 (VegVault 1.0.0 used the download of 26th June 2023). All data acquisition and processing have been done using the FOSSILPOL: Workflow for processing and standardizing global paleoecological pollen data (version 1.0.0), with the settings of VegVault 1.0.0. This includes the selection of depositional environments, ecological groups, chronology control point types, and a minimum number of chronology control points to construct age-depth models. Individual samples and records have been filtered by age limits, number of pollen grains, maximum age interpolation, and number of valid levels. In addition, the accuracy of fossil pollen data is increased by re-estimating all age-depth models using the Bayesian probabilistic approach and including the information about individual age uncertainty. Age-depth models of VegVault 1.0.0 are reused for records whose chronology did not change since the 2023 download, and fitted again for the others.
Selection Criteria:

Only records with type “pollen” with valid geological coordinates (longitude between -180 and 180, latitude between -90 and 90)
Depositional environments: lakes, bogs, and mires only (selection table)
Specific ecological groups retained (selection tables)
Minimum 5 chronology control points (valid types)

Quality Filters:

Minimum 125 pollen grains per sample (balanced for data retention vs. quality)

While the preferred minimum was initially set at 150, this threshold resulted in significant data loss
Threshold adjusted to 125 with condition that less than 75% of samples would have low pollen sum

Age limits: 0-20,000 cal yr BP
Exclusion of samples older than 3000 years of the last chronology control point
Minimum 5 samples per record
Re-calculated age-depth models using Bayesian approach {Bchron} package

Processing Details: Available at VegVault-FOSSILPOL



The primary sources of contemporary plot-based vegetation data are BIEN (Botanical Information and Ecology Network) and sPlotOpen (the open-access version of sPlot).
BIEN Processing:

Downloaded using {BIEN} R package v1.2.8 on 20th November 2026 from BIEN database 4.2.8, the database version of VegVault 1.0.0, using function BIEN::BIEN_plot_datasource()
Retained key columns: datasource_id, datasource, plot_name, sampling_protocol, methodology_reference, methodology_description, longitude, latitude, plot_area_ha, subplot, individual_count, family_matched, name_matched, name_matched_author, verbatim_family, verbatim_scientific_name, scrubbed_species_binomial, scrubbed_taxonomic_status, scrubbed_family, scrubbed_author
All columns renamed using snake case
Filtered out records with missing essential information (NA values in datasource_id, datasource, plot_name, longitude, latitude, and/or plot_area_ha)
Records of one taxon (name_matched) in a plot merged into one record, with their individual counts added
Only the latest survey kept for plots surveyed more than once
One row per plot, with a stable plot identifier plot_id

sPlotOpen Processing:

sPlotOpen v2.0, downloaded on 26th September 2023 for VegVault 1.0.0 and kept, as no newer open release exists
Linked tables DT2.oa and header.oa via PlotObservationID column
Applied quality filters for geographic and area data (filtered out rows with NA values in PlotObservationID, GIVD_ID, Longitude, Latitude, and/or Releve_area)
Records without a species name dropped, and records of one species in a plot merged into one record
All columns renamed using snake case

Processing Details: Available at VegVault-Vegetation_data



Following Díaz et al. (2016), we selected six key functional traits representing:

Stem specific density
Leaf nitrogen content per unit mass
Diaspore mass
Plant height
Leaf area
Leaf mass per area

TRY Database Processing:

Data request ID: 28498 on 29th August 2023, the request of VegVault 1.0.0 (no new request was made)
Requested traits with codes: 3106, 4, 3108, 3110, 3112, 3114, 3116, 3117, 14, and 26 (closest to Díaz et al. 2016 description)
The request file is read with the same settings as rtry::rtry_import()
For each trait (TraitID), extracted all relevant observations (ObservationID), ensuring only observations unique to each trait
Identified all unique data (DataID) associated with each trait
Excluded non-meaningful trait variations (DataID: 2221, 2222, 2223, 2224, 2225, 3646, 3647, 3698, 3699, 3727, 3728, 3730, 3731, 3849, 3850, 4029, and 4030), e.g., height at 15 days
Extracted covariate information (additional data stored in DataName column)
Trait values taken from TRY’s standardised values (StdValue)
Removed records that TRY flags as copies of another record, and repeated values of one trait within one observation
Impossible, unparsable or incomplete coordinates set to missing
All columns renamed using snake case
Added Trait Domain variable to group traits following Díaz et al. (2016) selection for efficient extraction across TRY and BIEN

BIEN Traits Processing:

Downloaded using {BIEN} R package v1.2.8 on 19th November 2026 from BIEN database 4.2.8, using function BIEN::BIEN_trait_trait()
Requested traits: whole plant height, stem wood density, leaf area, leaf area per leaf dry mass, leaf nitrogen content per leaf dry mass, and seed mass
Retained columns: trait_name, trait_value, unit, id, longitude, latitude, method, url_source, source_citation, project_pi, scrubbed_species_binomial, and access
Removed records from sources that copy a compilation held by TRY and match a published TRY record (the TRY copy is kept)

Units and quality checks (both providers):

Every value converted to the single unit of its trait domain by a registered and versioned rule; values whose unit is not registered, or whose conversion fails, are not published
leaf mass per area derived from specific leaf area (leaf area per leaf dry mass) as 1/value, after the specific leaf area is converted to a known unit
Values from sources whose scale is physically implausible not published

Processing Details: Available at VegVault-Trait_data



The primary sources of abiotic data are CHELSA, CHELSA-TRACE21, and the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD) v2.2. The first two data sources provide high-resolution downscaled climatic data, while the latter offers detailed soil information (only available for contemporary data). VegVault 1.0.0 used HWSD v2.0 or v2.01 (the exact version was not recorded) and named it WoSIS or SoilGrids.
CHELSA Climate Data:

Contemporary: CHELSA v2.1, all seven files downloaded on 20th November 2026 (VegVault 1.0.0: 8th September 2023)
Used {ClimDatDownloadR} R package with function ClimDatDownloadR::Chelsa.Clim.download()
Selected bio-variables: 1, 4, 6, 12, 15, 18, 19
Spatial aggregation: 25x factor using median values with {terra} R package function terra::aggregate(factor = 25, fun = "median")
bio4 (temperature seasonality) in hundredths of a degree Celsius; in VegVault 1.0.0 it was 0 south of about 65.7° N because of a truncated download
A bio12 value of 6553.5 is the storage limit of CHELSA V2.1, so it is a lower bound

Paleoclimate: CHELSA-TRACE21

Paleoclimate: CHELSA-TRACE21 v1.0, the files downloaded on 31st December 2023 for VegVault 1.0.0, with bio15 at age 0 downloaded again on 20th November 2026 (in VegVault 1.0.0 it was 0 south of 14.65° S because of a truncated download)
Downloaded values for each 500-year time-slice between 0 and 18,000 years before present (BP)
Selected bio-variables: 1, 4, 6, 12, 15, 18, 19
For each time slice, applied spatial aggregation using terra::aggregate(factor = 25, fun = "median")
Inflated precipitation of the source in 25° S to 5° N and 80° W to 35° W, at 12,000, 12,500 and 15,000 to 18,000 years, masked: there, bio12, bio15, bio18 and bio19 have no value
Precipitation stored in whole kg m-2, so a quarter with less than 0.5 kg m-2 is 0

HWSD Soil Data:

HWSD v2.2 downloaded on 20th November 2026 (both hwsd2.2_raster.zip and hwsd2.2_db.zip); VegVault 1.0.0 used HWSD v2.0 or v2.01, downloaded on 11th September 2023
Soil groups: the WRB 2022 Reference Soil Group of each cell, coded 1 to 32 in alphabetical order; a cell whose dominant class is not a soil (glaciers, open water) has no value
The soil codes of VegVault 1.0.0 came from a wrong lookup and cannot be compared with those of v2.0.0
Resampled using terra::resample(method = "near") function to match climate data resolution
Provides essential edaphic context for vegetation-environment relationships (contemporary data only)

Processing Details: Available at VegVault-abiotic_data




All processing pipelines with their corresponding Tags are migrated into an SQLite database using the GitHub repository titled VegVault, which can be accessed as DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14777447 (all versions). The build is a {targets} pipeline in six stages: import of the pinned files, links between samples and gridpoints, assembly of the database, validation, export of the flat files, and the figures of the data paper.


Migrating sPlotOpen vegetation data:

Dataset name (dataset_name) created from plot_observation_id as splot_[plot_observation_id]
Original data source from column givd_id stored in DatasetSourcesID table
Sample name (sample_name) created using plot_observation_id as splot_[plot_observation_id]
Sample Size (sample_size) created from releve_area column
All samples automatically assigned age of 0
Taxonomic names extracted from Species column, abundances from Original_abundance; records without a species name are not stored

Migrating BIEN vegetation data:

Dataset name (dataset_name) created from the plot identifier as bien_[plot_id] (VegVault 1.0.0 used the row number of the file, which changes when rows are added or reordered)
Original data source from column datasource stored in DatasetSourcesID table
Sampling method extracted from methodology_description column
Sample name (sample_name) created as bien_[plot_id]
Sample Size (sample_size) created from plot_area_ha column, multiplied by 10,000 (stored in square meters)
All samples automatically assigned age of 0
Taxonomic names extracted from name_matched column

Migrating fossil pollen data:

Dataset name (dataset_name) created from the Neotoma dataset identifier as fossilpol_[dataset_id]
Note: the Neotoma dataset_id in the name is not the dataset_id of the VegVault table Datasets, which is numbered anew in every build
Original data source from source_of_data column stored in DatasetSourcesID table
Sampling method extracted from depositionalenvironment column
Individual Dataset Reference extracted from doi column
Sample name (sample_name) created from the Neotoma identifiers of the dataset and the sample as fossilpol_[dataset_id]_[sample_id] (VegVault 1.0.0 used the database identifier of the dataset here, so sample names changed with every build)
Ages extracted from levels column
Age uncertainty from age-depth models extracted from age_uncertainty column
Taxonomic names and abundances extracted from counts_harmonised column; a taxon is stored for a sample only when its count is above zero

Migrating TRY functional traits:

Dataset name (dataset_name) created as try_[number]: one dataset per combination of data source, longitude, latitude and reference, numbered in the order of these values (VegVault 1.0.0 numbered them in the order of the file)
Original data source from column dataset stored in DatasetSourcesID table
Individual Dataset Reference extracted from reference_source column
Sample name (sample_name) created from the TRY observation as try_[observation_id]
Individual Sample references extracted from dataset_reference_citation and record_reference (the publication of each TRY record)
All samples automatically assigned age of 0
Trait names extracted from trait_full_name, taxonomic names from acc_species_name, trait values from trait_value, with their unit and conversion rule

Migrating BIEN functional traits:

Dataset name (dataset_name) created as bien_traits_[number], by the same rule as for TRY
Original data source from column project_pi stored in DatasetSourcesID table
Individual Dataset Reference extracted from source_citation column
Sample name (sample_name) created using column id as bien_traits_[id]
All samples automatically assigned age of 0
Trait names extracted from trait_full_name, taxonomic names from scrubbed_species_binomial, trait values from trait_value, with their unit and conversion rule




In addition to the consolidation of all processed data into a unified SQLite database, the final VegVault migration repository performs three critical procedures to ensure data consistency and usability:


As VegVault integrates data on taxa from various sources, the {taxospace} R package is used to classify diverse taxa into a unifying taxonomic backbone. The {taxospace} tool automatically aligns taxon names with the GBIF taxonomical backbone. Specifically, we find the best match of raw taxon names using the Global Names Verifier, which is then aligned with GBIF. Only plant taxa count, each name is sent with only its first letter in capitals, and when a name matches several taxa equally well, the taxon with the smallest GBIF identifier is used. The resulting taxonomic classification information, detailed up to the family level, is stored for each taxon, ensuring consistency and facilitating comparative analyses across different datasets.
Two kinds of names are corrected by hand after the automatic classification. Fossil pollen types that combine two or more taxa (such as the Neotoma name “Betula/Carpinus”, stored as “Betula Carpinus”) keep only what their parts share: the family when all parts belong to one family, and no classification otherwise. The pollen type “Pinus Picea” is classified as the family Pinaceae, the family of both genera, instead of Abies alba, to which the automatic matching resolves it.
Important limitations: Taxonomic classification down to the species level is not available for each taxon (e.g., some fossil pollen types can only be identified to the genus or family level). For several taxa, no matching classification could be found. Note that taxonomic classification is additional information—the original taxon name is always present and returned by default. Finally, users should be aware that this classification is an automated process and may contain errors.



As there are differences in trait names across data sources (e.g., “Leaf nitrogen (N) content per leaf dry mass” vs. “leaf nitrogen content per leaf dry mass”), we added a new variable Trait Domain that groups traits together following the trait selection of Díaz et al. (2016). For example, trait Plant height vegetative from TRY and trait whole plant height from BIEN are both grouped under the Trait Domain stored as Plant heigh, the spelling of VegVault 1.0.0. This grouping serves as an efficient mechanism for extracting comparable traits across both TRY and BIEN datasets. Every trait value is stored in the unit of its Trait Domain, together with the rule that converted it.



We developed a data structure that provides readily available environmental context for each vegetation (and trait) record by creating spatio-temporal links between these records and abiotic information. As raster data are not suitable for storage in an SQLite database, we created artificial points, called ‘gridpoints’, located in the center of each raster cell. This resulted in a uniform spatio-temporal matrix of gridpoints holding the abiotic information.
Gridpoint naming conventions: dataset_name are created as “geo_[longitude][latitude]” and sample_name are created as ”geo[longitude][latitude][age]”.
Spatial-temporal linking: We linked gridpoints with every other non-gridpoint Sample (vegetation_plot, fossil_pollen_archive, and traits) that lies at most 50 km and at most 5,000 years from it, and discarded the gridpoint Samples without such a link. The distance is the geodesic distance on the WGS84 ellipsoid; the distance and the age difference are stored truncated to whole kilometres and years. Since v2.0.0 the rule is applied exactly: VegVault 1.0.0 searched only within one degree of longitude and did not wrap at the dateline, so it missed the links at high latitudes, where 50 km is more than one degree of longitude, and across the dateline. The links are computed and stored once per position, a distinct combination of longitude, latitude and age (tables Positions, SamplePosition and PositionLink), and the view AbioticDataReference returns them per sample, as the table of the same name did in VegVault 1.0.0.

title: Data Assembly Process of VegVault 2.0.0
text:
All processing pipelines with their corresponding Tags are migrated into an SQLite database using the GitHub repository titled VegVault, which can be accessed as DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14777447 (all versions). The build is a {targets} pipeline in six stages: import of the pinned files, links between samples and gridpoints, assembly of the database, validation, export of the flat files, and the figures of the data paper.


Migrating sPlotOpen vegetation data:

Dataset name (dataset_name) created from plot_observation_id as splot_[plot_observation_id]
Original data source from column givd_id stored in DatasetSourcesID table
Sample name (sample_name) created using plot_observation_id as splot_[plot_observation_id]
Sample Size (sample_size) created from releve_area column
All samples automatically assigned age of 0
Taxonomic names extracted from Species column, abundances from Original_abundance; records without a species name are not stored

Migrating BIEN vegetation data:

Dataset name (dataset_name) created from the plot identifier as bien_[plot_id] (VegVault 1.0.0 used the row number of the file, which changes when rows are added or reordered)
Original data source from column datasource stored in DatasetSourcesID table
Sampling method extracted from methodology_description column
Sample name (sample_name) created as bien_[plot_id]
Sample Size (sample_size) created from plot_area_ha column, multiplied by 10,000 (stored in square meters)
All samples automatically assigned age of 0
Taxonomic names extracted from name_matched column

Migrating fossil pollen data:

Dataset name (dataset_name) created from the Neotoma dataset identifier as fossilpol_[dataset_id]
Note: the Neotoma dataset_id in the name is not the dataset_id of the VegVault table Datasets, which is numbered anew in every build
Original data source from source_of_data column stored in DatasetSourcesID table
Sampling method extracted from depositionalenvironment column
Individual Dataset Reference extracted from doi column
Sample name (sample_name) created from the Neotoma identifiers of the dataset and the sample as fossilpol_[dataset_id]_[sample_id] (VegVault 1.0.0 used the database identifier of the dataset here, so sample names changed with every build)
Ages extracted from levels column
Age uncertainty from age-depth models extracted from age_uncertainty column
Taxonomic names and abundances extracted from counts_harmonised column; a taxon is stored for a sample only when its count is above zero

Migrating TRY functional traits:

Dataset name (dataset_name) created as try_[number]: one dataset per combination of data source, longitude, latitude and reference, numbered in the order of these values (VegVault 1.0.0 numbered them in the order of the file)
Original data source from column dataset stored in DatasetSourcesID table
Individual Dataset Reference extracted from reference_source column
Sample name (sample_name) created from the TRY observation as try_[observation_id]
Individual Sample references extracted from dataset_reference_citation and record_reference (the publication of each TRY record)
All samples automatically assigned age of 0
Trait names extracted from trait_full_name, taxonomic names from acc_species_name, trait values from trait_value, with their unit and conversion rule

Migrating BIEN functional traits:

Dataset name (dataset_name) created as bien_traits_[number], by the same rule as for TRY
Original data source from column project_pi stored in DatasetSourcesID table
Individual Dataset Reference extracted from source_citation column
Sample name (sample_name) created using column id as bien_traits_[id]
All samples automatically assigned age of 0
Trait names extracted from trait_full_name, taxonomic names from scrubbed_species_binomial, trait values from trait_value, with their unit and conversion rule




In addition to the consolidation of all processed data into a unified SQLite database, the final VegVault migration repository performs three critical procedures to ensure data consistency and usability:


As VegVault integrates data on taxa from various sources, the {taxospace} R package is used to classify diverse taxa into a unifying taxonomic backbone. The {taxospace} tool automatically aligns taxon names with the GBIF taxonomical backbone. Specifically, we find the best match of raw taxon names using the Global Names Verifier, which is then aligned with GBIF. Only plant taxa count, each name is sent with only its first letter in capitals, and when a name matches several taxa equally well, the taxon with the smallest GBIF identifier is used. The resulting taxonomic classification information, detailed up to the family level, is stored for each taxon, ensuring consistency and facilitating comparative analyses across different datasets.
Two kinds of names are corrected by hand after the automatic classification. Fossil pollen types that combine two or more taxa (such as the Neotoma name “Betula/Carpinus”, stored as “Betula Carpinus”) keep only what their parts share: the family when all parts belong to one family, and no classification otherwise. The pollen type “Pinus Picea” is classified as the family Pinaceae, the family of both genera, instead of Abies alba, to which the automatic matching resolves it.
Important limitations: Taxonomic classification down to the species level is not available for each taxon (e.g., some fossil pollen types can only be identified to the genus or family level). For several taxa, no matching classification could be found. Note that taxonomic classification is additional information—the original taxon name is always present and returned by default. Finally, users should be aware that this classification is an automated process and may contain errors.



As there are differences in trait names across data sources (e.g., “Leaf nitrogen (N) content per leaf dry mass” vs. “leaf nitrogen content per leaf dry mass”), we added a new variable Trait Domain that groups traits together following the trait selection of Díaz et al. (2016). For example, trait Plant height vegetative from TRY and trait whole plant height from BIEN are both grouped under the Trait Domain stored as Plant heigh, the spelling of VegVault 1.0.0. This grouping serves as an efficient mechanism for extracting comparable traits across both TRY and BIEN datasets. Every trait value is stored in the unit of its Trait Domain, together with the rule that converted it.



We developed a data structure that provides readily available environmental context for each vegetation (and trait) record by creating spatio-temporal links between these records and abiotic information. As raster data are not suitable for storage in an SQLite database, we created artificial points, called ‘gridpoints’, located in the center of each raster cell. This resulted in a uniform spatio-temporal matrix of gridpoints holding the abiotic information.
Gridpoint naming conventions: dataset_name are created as “geo_[longitude][latitude]” and sample_name are created as ”geo[longitude][latitude][age]”.
Spatial-temporal linking: We linked gridpoints with every other non-gridpoint Sample (vegetation_plot, fossil_pollen_archive, and traits) that lies at most 50 km and at most 5,000 years from it, and discarded the gridpoint Samples without such a link. The distance is the geodesic distance on the WGS84 ellipsoid; the distance and the age difference are stored truncated to whole kilometres and years. Since v2.0.0 the rule is applied exactly: VegVault 1.0.0 searched only within one degree of longitude and did not wrap at the dateline, so it missed the links at high latitudes, where 50 km is more than one degree of longitude, and across the dateline. The links are computed and stored once per position, a distinct combination of longitude, latitude and age (tables Positions, SamplePosition and PositionLink), and the view AbioticDataReference returns them per sample, as the table of the same name did in VegVault 1.0.0.

title: VegVault
text:
This is the official website dedicated to the VegVault project. VegVault is a comprehensive SQLite database that integrates global paleo- and neo-ecological vegetation data with functional traits and abiotic information, including climate and soil data. By bridging historical and contemporary data across multiple temporal and spatial scales, VegVault provides a unique resource for examining long-term ecological patterns and processes, thereby enhancing our ability to predict future biodiversity trajectories and ecosystem responses under changing climatic conditions.
The project integrates data from multiple well-established sources including the Neotoma Paleoecology Database, sPlotOpen, BIEN, TRY Plant Trait Database, CHELSA climate data, and the Harmonized World Soil Database to provide a comprehensive view of vegetation dynamics across space and time.
Creating such an integrated database, in which gathering and processing of the data is reproducible, is a crucial step toward improving our understanding of biodiversity dynamics under changing climatic conditions and safeguarding biodiversity in an uncertain future.
The project is part of the BIODYNAMICS project.

title: Database Access & Usage
text:
VegVault 2.0.0 is available as a comprehensive SQLite database providing integrated access to global vegetation, trait, and environmental data. What changed between versions, and what it means for code written for an earlier version, is on the changelog page.
Download VegVault (latest version)
The button leads to the newest version of the SQLite database in the EOSC CZ data repository; the current version is VegVault 2.0.0. Earlier versions stay available there, and the changelog page gives the DOI of each version.






Note



System Requirements: The VegVault 2.0.0 database is a single file of 6.1 GiB. Ensure your system has sufficient storage space and memory (RAM) before downloading.




For users who prefer working with individual data tables, we provide VegVault as separate CSV files:
Download VegVault flat files (latest version)






Warning



Note: Flat files are not the recommended approach. The 34 table files hold 5.3 GiB together, and the largest 2 exceed 1 GB, which may be difficult to load into memory. The links between samples and grid points are stored once per position, so the flat files have no AbioticDataReference table: join SamplePosition and PositionLink by position_id to get the grid points of each sample. We strongly recommend using the SQLite database with the {vaultkeepr} R package for optimal performance.








To make VegVault easily accessible, we developed {vaultkeepr}, a well-tested R package (>95% code coverage) that provides intuitive functions for interacting with the database. The package handles database connections, data filtering, and extraction, allowing you to retrieve only project-specific data without loading everything into memory.














Install {vaultkeepr} from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("OndrejMottl/vaultkeepr")

Load the package:

library(vaultkeepr)




See our Usage Examples for detailed demonstrations of how to:

Extract vegetation data for specific regions and time periods
Access functional trait information
Link abiotic environmental data
Perform taxonomic harmonization







VegVault is released under CC BY 4.0 License (Creative Commons Attribution 4.0), allowing you to:

Copy and redistribute the material
Adapt and build upon the material

Requirements: You must provide appropriate attribution to VegVault and cite all primary data sources.



When using VegVault in your research:

Cite VegVault: Always cite the VegVault version you used with its corresponding DOI, and the VegVault data paper
Cite primary sources: Acknowledge all original data providers included in your analysis
Use our helper function: The vaultkeepr::get_references() function automatically generates the complete list of recommended citations for your specific data compilation




Data paper: “VegVault dataset: linking global paleo-, and neo-vegetation data with functional traits and abiotic drivers”
Read the Data Paper
Pre-print (the earlier version of the data paper): “VegVault database: linking global paleo-, and neo-vegetation data with functional traits and abiotic drivers”
Access Pre-print
For additional citation materials, visit our Materials & Outputs page.






VegVault’s quality depends on the completeness, accuracy, and reliability of primary data sources. We acknowledge potential issues in global ecological databases (as noted for TRY) but focus on improving data re-usability rather than correcting source data quality issues.




Storage requirements: the 6.1 GiB database file may be challenging for some systems
Memory requirements: Large datasets may require substantial RAM for analysis
Version dependencies: Always specify the VegVault version used in your research

VegVault 2.0.0 is the second release. Links are stored once per position. A position is a place and age shared by samples. The view AbioticDataReference returns 2,007,681,491 links in 2.0.0, against 2,067,445,952 rows of the table in 1.0.0. The unit label of bio4 is now “C/100 (hundredths of a degree Celsius)”, which matches its values; in 1.0.0 it read “C (degree Celsius)”. The values themselves were already in hundredths of a degree.
Present-day annual precipitation (bio12) of 6,553.5 kg m⁻² is a lower bound. CHELSA V2.1 stores it as whole numbers of 0.1 kg m⁻² of at most 65,535, so wetter places are stored as 6,553.5 kg m⁻² (note on VegVault issue 84). This is unchanged from 1.0.0, and now documented.
A precipitation artefact of CHELSA-TraCE21k is masked: bio12, bio15, bio18 and bio19 have no value in a block of South America (25° S to 5° N, 80° W to 35° W) at 12,000, 12,500 and 15,000 to 18,000 years before present, where the source shows inflated precipitation (note on VegVault issue 84).
Zero precipitation in dry seasons: CHELSA-TraCE21k stores precipitation in whole kg m⁻², so a quarter with less than 0.5 kg m⁻² is 0 in the past, while the present-day values come in steps of 0.1 kg m⁻² (check on VegVault issue 96). In the Sahel and the Sudanian belt, the coldest quarter of bio19 can be the dry winter in one product and the rainy season in the other.
Soil groups are rebuilt from HWSD v2.2; 1.0.0 labelled them WoSIS and SoilGrids. The codes 1 to 32 of HWSD2 are the WRB 2022 Reference Soil Groups in alphabetical order, and they cannot be compared with the codes of 1.0.0, which came from a wrong lookup (note on VegVault issue 84). The legend is Outputs/Tables/hwsd_soil_group_legend.csv in the abiotic data repository. A gridpoint whose dominant class is not a soil (glaciers, open water) has no soil value. 2.0.0 has 83,925 soil values at gridpoints, against 73,808 in 1.0.0.

Keys and checks: dataset and sample names are unique and never empty, the link and reference tables have composite primary keys, trait values are keyed on dataset, sample, trait and taxon, and coordinates must lie on the globe. Of the 59 secondary indexes of 1.0.0, the 29 that repeat another index or key are dropped (database design, decision 3).
Unchanged on purpose: the misspelt column trait_domanin_description of TraitsDomain, and the storage of gridpoints as datasets and samples.




A sample is linked to a gridpoint when the two are at most 50 km and at most 5,000 years apart. 1.0.0 used the same rule, but searched only within one degree of longitude and did not wrap at the dateline, so it missed some links. 2.0.0 applies the rule exactly. Run on the 1.0.0 inputs, it keeps every link of 1.0.0, with the same distances, and adds 427,097 links (0.45%) at 6,572 positions: 420,983 at high latitudes, where 50 km is more than one degree of longitude, and 6,114 across the dateline (comparison on VegVault issue 84).
The view AbioticDataReference returns 2,007,681,491 links in 2.0.0, against 2,067,445,952 rows of the table in 1.0.0. Because the rule of 2.0.0 keeps every link of 1.0.0 on the same inputs, the lower total comes from the samples of 2.0.0, which differ from those of 1.0.0 (see the sections below).




bio4 (temperature seasonality) is corrected. In 1.0.0 it was 0 at age 0 at every gridpoint south of about 65.7° N, because of a truncated download (VegVault issue 78). This affects every vegetation plot and every fossil pollen sample that takes its climate from age 0.
The unit label of bio4 is now “C/100 (hundredths of a degree Celsius)”, which matches its values; in 1.0.0 it read “C (degree Celsius)”. The values themselves were already in hundredths of a degree.
Present-day annual precipitation (bio12) of 6,553.5 kg m⁻² is a lower bound. CHELSA V2.1 stores it as whole numbers of 0.1 kg m⁻² of at most 65,535, so wetter places are stored as 6,553.5 kg m⁻² (note on VegVault issue 84). This is unchanged from 1.0.0, and now documented.
A precipitation artefact of CHELSA-TraCE21k is masked: bio12, bio15, bio18 and bio19 have no value in a block of South America (25° S to 5° N, 80° W to 35° W) at 12,000, 12,500 and 15,000 to 18,000 years before present, where the source shows inflated precipitation (note on VegVault issue 84).
Zero precipitation in dry seasons: CHELSA-TraCE21k stores precipitation in whole kg m⁻², so a quarter with less than 0.5 kg m⁻² is 0 in the past, while the present-day values come in steps of 0.1 kg m⁻² (check on VegVault issue 96). In the Sahel and the Sudanian belt, the coldest quarter of bio19 can be the dry winter in one product and the rainy season in the other.
Soil groups are rebuilt from HWSD v2.2; 1.0.0 labelled them WoSIS and SoilGrids. The codes 1 to 32 of HWSD2 are the WRB 2022 Reference Soil Groups in alphabetical order, and they cannot be compared with the codes of 1.0.0, which came from a wrong lookup (note on VegVault issue 84). The legend is Outputs/Tables/hwsd_soil_group_legend.csv in the abiotic data repository. A gridpoint whose dominant class is not a soil (glaciers, open water) has no soil value. 2.0.0 has 83,925 soil values at gridpoints, against 73,808 in 1.0.0.





Every trait value is in one unit per trait domain, converted from the unit of its source by a recorded rule. TraitUnitConversion holds 65 conversion rules and TraitDerivation 1 derivation rule (leaf mass per area from specific leaf area). Some values differ from 1.0.0 by a unit factor; for example, leaf area is now in mm² instead of cm².
The audit of the units is attached to the trait data release: a summary and a reconciliation of the units of each source (trait_unit_audit_summary_*.csv and trait_unit_reconciliation_*.csv), with the tables of the other checks of the trait data (VegVault issue 76).
TRY is kept, with TRY’s standardised values. In 1.0.0, 45.6% of the TRY values did not match the standardised value of their record. Repeated measurements are removed, including BIEN records that copy TRY (trait data release notes). The TRY reference of each record is stored as a sample reference.
Counts: 897,183 TRY values in 28,272 datasets (1.0.0: 1,205,168 in 32,342), and 10,023,769 BIEN values in 194,183 datasets (1.0.0: 10,161,055 in 194,788). BIEN trait samples without a value are dropped (database design, decision 4).
BIEN trait records that name no provider have no data source. The data source of a BIEN trait record is the principal investigator of its BIEN project, and 7,869 BIEN plant-height values in 3,609 datasets name none. In 2.0.0 their data_source_id is empty; in 1.0.0 they pointed to a data source without a description, so neither version names their provider (check on VegVault issue 167). {vaultkeepr} returns NA as their data_source_desc in both versions, but code that joins every dataset to a data source drops these records in 2.0.0.





Fossil pollen: a fresh download of the Neotoma Paleoecology Database and a full rerun of the FOSSILPOL workflow give 1,551 datasets with 100,341 samples, against 1,393 and 88,423 in 1.0.0 (FOSSILPOL release notes).
Vegetation plots: every plot has at most one record per taxon, and re-surveyed BIEN plots keep only their latest survey: 24,161 BIEN plots with 524,439 taxon records, against 24,233 and 972,791 in 1.0.0, and the same 67,022 sPlotOpen plots in both versions (vegetation data release notes).
Taxon names are classified again. Two kinds of names are corrected by hand: the 116 fossil pollen types that combine two or more taxa (such as “Betula/Carpinus”) keep only what their parts share, the family when all parts belong to one family (80 types) and no classification otherwise (36 types), and “Pinus Picea” is classified as Pinaceae instead of Abies alba (decision record on VegVault issue 86). Some errors of 1.0.0 are gone: for example, 1.0.0 classified the pollen type Alnus viridis as the genus Atanus, a leafhopper (comparison on vaultkeepr issue 51).
Unclassified names: 900 of the 109,220 taxon names (0.8%) have no classification.

title: VegVault Changelog
text: The first release of VegVault, described in the VegVault data paper. Its SQLite database (10.48700/datst.t21cz-2nq07) and its flat files (10.48700/datst.thktf-5rr35) are deposited in the EOSC CZ data repository.

title: VegVault Usage Examples
text:
To make VegVault as accessible as possible, we developed {vaultkeepr}, a comprehensive R package providing intuitive functions for interacting with the database. The package handles database connections, data filtering, and extraction, allowing you to retrieve only project-specific data without loading everything into memory. With >95% code coverage, {vaultkeepr} is a well-tested interface for VegVault.















Install {vaultkeepr} from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("OndrejMottl/vaultkeepr")

Load the package:

library(vaultkeepr)




The following diagram illustrates the systematic workflow for accessing and extracting data from VegVault using {vaultkeepr}:












Get the VegVault database: download the SQLite file.
Get the {vaultkeepr} R package: install it from GitHub as shown above. In R, every query then opens the database with vaultkeepr::open_vault() and starts from its datasets with vaultkeepr::get_datasets().
Choose the dataset types: keep vegetation_plot, fossil_pollen_archive, traits or gridpoints with vaultkeepr::select_dataset_by_type().
Choose the area and the time period:

Area: keep the datasets within a range of latitude and longitude with vaultkeepr::select_dataset_by_geo()
Samples: add the samples of these datasets with vaultkeepr::get_samples()
Time period: keep the samples within an age range with vaultkeepr::select_samples_by_age()

Choose the attributes to include:

Taxa: vaultkeepr::get_taxa(), with options for taxonomic harmonization
Traits: vaultkeepr::get_traits(), filtered by trait domain with vaultkeepr::select_traits_by_domain_name()
Abiotic data: vaultkeepr::get_abiotic_data(), with options for linking samples to gridpoints in space and time

Extract the data and references: vaultkeepr::extract_data() returns the data, and vaultkeepr::get_references() the references to cite.





The following examples demonstrate VegVault’s capabilities across different research scenarios. Note that these examples focus on data extraction rather than analysis—they show how to obtain properly formatted datasets for your research projects.



The first example demonstrates how to retrieve data for the genus Picea across North America by selecting both modern and fossil pollen plot datasets, filtering samples by geographic boundaries and temporal range (0 to 15,000 yr BP), and harmonizing taxa to the genus level. The resulting dataset allows users to study spatiotemporal patterns of Picea distribution over millennia. This can be accomplished by running the following code:
data_na_plots_picea <-
  # Access the VegVault
  vaultkeepr::open_vault(path = "<path_to_VegVault>") %>%
  # Start by adding dataset information
  vaultkeepr::get_datasets() %>%
  # Select both modern and paleo plot data
  vaultkeepr::select_dataset_by_type(
    sel_dataset_type = c(
      "vegetation_plot",
      "fossil_pollen_archive"
    )
  ) %>%
  # Limit data to North America
  vaultkeepr::select_dataset_by_geo(
    lat_lim = c(22, 60),
    long_lim = c(-135, -60)
  ) %>%
  # Add samples
  vaultkeepr::get_samples() %>%
  # Limit the samples by age
  vaultkeepr::select_samples_by_age(
    age_lim = c(0, 15e3)
  ) %>%
  # Add taxa & classify all data to a genus level
  vaultkeepr::get_taxa(classify_to = "genus") %>%
  # Extract only Picea data
  vaultkeepr::select_taxa_by_name(sel_taxa = "Picea") %>%
  vaultkeepr::extract_data()
Now, we plot the presence of Picea in each 2500-year bin.




In the second example, the project aims to do species distribution modelling for plant taxa in the Czech Republic based on contemporary vegetation plot data and mean annual temperature. The code includes selecting datasets and extracting relevant abiotic data as followed:
data_cz_modern <-
  # Acess the VegVault file
  vaultkeepr::open_vault(path = "<path_to_VegVault>") %>%
  # Add the dataset information
  vaultkeepr::get_datasets() %>%
  # Select modern plot data and climate
  vaultkeepr::select_dataset_by_type(
    sel_dataset_type = c(
      "vegetation_plot",
      "gridpoints"
    )
  ) %>%
  # Limit data to Czech Republic
  vaultkeepr::select_dataset_by_geo(
    lat_lim = c(48.5, 51.1),
    long_lim = c(12, 18.9)
  ) %>%
  # Add samples
  vaultkeepr::get_samples() %>%
  # select only modern data
  vaultkeepr::select_samples_by_age(
    age_lim = c(0, 0)
  ) %>%
  # Add abiotic data
  vaultkeepr::get_abiotic_data() %>%
  # Select only Mean Anual Temperature (bio1)
  vaultkeepr::select_abiotic_var_by_name(sel_var_name = "bio1") %>%
  # add taxa
  vaultkeepr::get_taxa() %>%
  vaultkeepr::extract_data()
Now we can simply plot both the climatic data and the plot vegetation data:




The third example focuses on obtaining data to be able to reconstruct plant height for South and Central America between 6-12 ka cal yr BP (thousand years before present). This example project showcases the integration of trait data with paleo-vegetation records to subsequently study historical vegetation dynamics and functional composition of plant communities:
data_la_traits <-
  # Acess the VegVault file
  vaultkeepr::open_vault(path = "<path_to_VegVault>") %>%
  # Add the dataset information
  vaultkeepr::get_datasets() %>%
  # Select modern plot data and climate
  vaultkeepr::select_dataset_by_type(
    sel_dataset_type = c(
      "fossil_pollen_archive",
      "traits"
    )
  ) %>%
  # Limit data to South and Central America
  vaultkeepr::select_dataset_by_geo(
    lat_lim = c(-53, 28),
    long_lim = c(-110, -38),
    sel_dataset_type = c(
      "fossil_pollen_archive",
      "traits"
    )
  ) %>%
  # Add samples
  vaultkeepr::get_samples() %>%
  # Limit to 6-12 ka yr BP
  vaultkeepr::select_samples_by_age(
    age_lim = c(6e3, 12e3)
  ) %>%
  # add taxa & clasify all data to a genus level
  vaultkeepr::get_taxa(classify_to = "genus") %>%
  # add trait information & clasify all data to a genus level
  vaultkeepr::get_traits(classify_to = "genus") %>%
  # Only select the plant height (the trait domain is stored as "Plant heigh")
  vaultkeepr::select_traits_by_domain_name(sel_domain = "Plant heigh") %>%
  vaultkeepr::extract_data()
Now let’s plot the overview of the data

text:
This page provides access to all VegVault-related resources including the database, publications, code, and presentation materials.






VegVault (SQLite Database - Recommended) Download VegVault (latest version)
The current version is VegVault 2.0.0; the changelog page gives the DOI of each version.
Please review our Database Access Guidelines for proper usage and citation requirements.















VegVault (Flat Files - Not Recommended) Download VegVault flat files (latest version)
